answer: Every action a quill signs is stamped onto a public ledger, so an attacker's fleet of fakes must each behave differently enough to escape fingerprint clustering. A lotus sharing water with its twins sinks with them: when the protocol links near-identical attestation patterns, the whole cluster is slashed, including rewards earned months earlier. The ocean keeps no secrets, and retroactive graph audits cost the attacker more than mining ever paid back, so spawning cheap copies loses money.
